After some centuries, the city's first and last king killed her with a sword. Her released power turned the people nearby into salt and the place was sealed. Survivors fled to Liyue Harbor, under Morax's protection.

Its descendants include the salt-trade guild Yinyuan Hall, which keeps a version of the story that Zhongli's quest shows to be distorted.

Established: The civilisation was ruled by Havria, God of Salt, who is described as the gentlest of the gods and a weak one. She would not take part in the Archon War and tried to buy peace by giving up land. According to Roald, she sheltered people dispossessed by the war, and they settled under her care and lived humbly. Zhongli adds that she searched all of Liyue for a haven for them, and the one she found is the place now called Sal Terrae. The settlement stood for some centuries, in Roald's account. By the end its territory had shrunk to a small underground refuge.

Roald's diary, written as a modern traveller's reading of the ruin, says the city centred on a temple and that most of the old city seems to have sunk into the Bishui River. Havria had two relics, a bottomless salt chalice that stays half-full and a ruler that covers the ground in salt when it is driven into the earth, both found in the sealed ruin during the story quest. A tradition recorded on the wiki, not re-read in the book text, links the Flower Ball custom to her habit of handing out flowers to her people.

Fall: The civilisation's first and last king killed Havria. Roald's diary says he had once loved her but sought military might and wanted to show that gentleness was unfit for the times. Zhongli tells it differently: some of her people reasoned that a quick release was kinder than being beaten, since she could not protect them. When a god dies, the power released is more than mortals can bear. Her body dissipated, leaving only a single flower of salt, and the people who could not escape were turned to salt, caught in postures of flight. The king's figure remains in the pose of the blow. The people outside the blast scattered across Liyue, and many went to Liyue Harbor, then under Morax's protection.

The ruin's inner rooms show the moment frozen in place. Salinised adherents are caught running toward the way out, and in the central room a figure that once held something upraised stands over the place where Havria died. A broken sword in two pieces lay in the ruin. Zhongli identifies it as the murder weapon, not a weapon of Havria's, since she had no blade left to defend her people with. Roald's diary adds a rumour that her salt body still keeps the posture of the instant she was struck; the quest shows nothing of her but the flower.

Aftermath: Descendants of the survivors feared that Havria had cursed them. They returned to the ruin, broke the sword, set it with two of her relics on a pedestal, and resealed the area, hoping for forgiveness. Zhongli says she bore them no hatred and would have understood their act. Over thousands of years the story was passed down in different forms. Yinyuan Hall, the Liyue Qixing's salt trade hall, now holds that Morax murdered Havria out of envy, as stated by its member Wanyan. Other families preserve the true tale, as Roald records. A stone stele at the entrance says that salt seals the ruin and that no uninvited person may enter. In the quest the seal opens only after a mechanism and four elemental monuments are activated in the order south, east, west, north, following an old riddle about Liyue's mountains.

Zhongli says Havria's fate served as a warning to him during the Archon War. At the end of the quest he tells Wanyan that faith in a god who has already died does her no good, and that this holds equally for Havria and for Morax. For ordinary scenes, Sal Terrae's people exist only as survivors' descendants and as the ruin; there is no living civilisation.

Open questions: Canon does not name the king, give the population or date the founding or fall of the city in years, beyond placing it in the Archon War several millennia ago (Roald). It also leaves open which account of the king's motive is accurate: Roald's ambitious king or Zhongli's mercy-minded followers. Canon does not describe the fate of the king beyond his frozen figure. Nothing from Nod-Krai or Snezhnaya content (Versions 6.x to 7.1) changes this entry.

Expedition: The ruin was opened by an expedition to Sal Terrae in Zhongli's story quest: the Snezhnayan Fatuus archaeologist Kliment hoped for treasure, and Wanyan of Yinyuan Hall hoped for proof of Morax's guilt. Zhongli served as consultant under a contract that let them claim relics in turn, one object per claim. Kliment took the chalice and then tried to break the contract over the ruler, and Zhongli removed him from the expedition. Wanyan broke the contract over the two sword halves and was given the truth as her penalty.

Connections: Related to Havria, the Sal Terrae location in Bishui Plain, Zhongli's Historia Antiqua story quest, Yinyuan Hall and the Eight Trades, Liyue Harbor, and the Archon War. Compare the Guili Assembly, another Liyue civilisation ended in the same war whose survivors also founded Liyue Harbor.

240.content:
Sal Terrae was the refuge of Havria, the gentle God of Salt, in Liyue's Bishui Plain. Her king killed her; the power released turned most of her people to salt, and survivors fled to Liyue Harbor. Its ruin is sealed and was opened in Zhongli's Sal Flore story quest (1.1).

Only Havria's remains in the form of a salt flower, two relics, a broken sword and the frozen figures of her adherents are left. Yinyuan Hall descends from the survivors.

241.comment: Sal Terrae (Civilization): Wanyan and the Yinyuan Hall legend
241.content: In the story quest, Wanyan of Yinyuan Hall believes that Morax killed the God of Salt out of envy and hopes to prove it. Zhongli's evidence shows the king killed her. Wanyan cannot accept this at first; Zhongli tells her it is the price of breaking their expedition contract, and the quest leaves her struggling with it.

242.content:
Khaenri'ah's Savior (also: Savior of Khaenri'ah, Khaenriah's Savior, the golden-haired Savior, Princess of Khaenri'ah, Prince of Khaenri'ah): "Savior" was the title Khaenri'ah's last king, Irmin, and his court gave to the Traveler's twin when he made them royal heir about five hundred years ago. The Khaenri'ahn people were told the heir would bring the kingdom prosperity and rescue it. Instead Irmin used the heir as a vessel for Abyssal power, and the kingdom was destroyed. The title lingers among descendants who still await a golden-haired Savior.

In the Natlan chapter (5.7) Direidyth, a young Khaenri'ahn from the time of the Cataclysm, is shown still searching for the Savior and calls the Traveler by the title; the Abyss Order's Haden recalls that everyone prayed for the Savior when the disaster struck and the heir was nowhere to be found.

Established: - The Traveler's twin fell into Teyvat separately from the Traveler, wandered the world looking for them, and arrived in the underground kingdom of Khaenri'ah.
- King Irmin, the last Vinster King of the Eclipse Dynasty, declared the twin his heir. They became the Princess (if the Traveler is male, Lumine) or Prince (if female, Aether) of Khaenri'ah, and a great celebration was held.
- The court of Khaenri'ah proclaimed the heir a source of hope who would bring the kingdom prosperity; "the Savior" was the celebratory title that grew from this. Dainsleif says in 5.7 that it was a title given by those who believed the court's rhetoric.
- Soon after, Irmin led the heir to the kingdom's deepest depths and used them as a vessel to absorb "unlimited" Abyssal power.

- The Wings of Fate's Course Intertwined glider text places a then-ordinary young knight, Dainsleif, in the plaza crowd at the announcement. The heir looked out over a populace they had not realised lived underground, having already lost their home world.
- Dainsleif was later promoted to captain of the Royal Guard with the title "Twilight Sword". He and the later Five Sinners stormed the palace to rescue his imprisoned brother Vedrfolnir, and the Abyssal power in the heir was divided among the five; Skirk's character story gives one-sixth each.
- The glider text calls the heir the key to the world's near-annihilation.

- The Savior role was never one the heir chose. In the 5.7 quests the heir says that when the Cataclysm began they were preparing to fight back, but news that the Traveler was alive led them to leave Khaenri'ah at its most critical moment; they say the choice haunted them for five hundred years and that it drives their devotion to restoring the nation.
- Irmin's advisers who distrusted forbidden knowledge did not persuade him to stop, according to Pierro's artifact text as summarised by the wiki.

- Direidyth says her grandmother begged her to leave her village and find the Savior before doomsday. The one detail she notes as not matching the Traveler is gender: her village's Savior is described as a young person of the opposite gender to the Traveler, which fits the Traveler's twin.

The announcement: The heir was presented to the people at a large celebration in the plaza before the palace gate. Irmin and the Court of Khaenri'ah proclaimed that the heir would bring great prosperity and began promoting them as a "Savior". The glider text says the heir, who had lost their own world, was now asked to carry the hopes of a single nation; Dainsleif watched from the crowd as an ordinary young knight and helped tidy the plaza afterwards.

The wiki gives the sequence as arrival in Khaenri'ah, appointment as heir and Prince/Princess, the celebration, then the vessel ritual soon after. How long the heir served before the ritual is not stated precisely; one wiki passage mentions "several years" as heir.

The Universitas Magistrorum is tied to the arrival only by a namecard line (Achievement: Orbits, 4.0) addressed to an "Almighty Sovereign", reporting predictions of two stars captured by the world's gravity whose paths would intertwine again. The wiki reads this as implying the Universitas predicted the twins' arrival at Irmin's request; the text itself names neither the twins nor Irmin directly.

The vessel: Irmin later led the heir to the kingdom's deepest depths and used them as a vessel for unlimited Abyssal power. His obsession with the Abyss was growing: the Universitas Magistrorum was reassigned to Abyssal research and the Crimson Moon bloodline was hunted. When Vedrfolnir warned that this path would end in the kingdom's fall, Irmin had his eyes gouged out and imprisoned him.

Dainsleif gathered Hroptatyr, Rhinedottir, Rerir and Surtalogi to free Vedrfolnir, and the rescue became a coup. The Abyssal power in the heir was split among Rhinedottir, Rerir, Vedrfolnir, Surtalogi and Hroptatyr, who became the Five Sinners of Khaenri'ah. Rhinedottir's creations then attacked Khaenri'ah and the nations of Teyvat, and the Heavenly Principles intervened.

The glider text frames the meeting of Dainsleif and the heir as an intersection of two paths: a noble falling from the light into the Abyss, and a humble knight climbing from the dark. After the Cataclysm the two travelled Teyvat together for a time, until the sibling realised the "truth of this world" and became Dainsleif's enemy, aligning with the Abyss Order.

The title after the fall: In the Natlan chapter, Direidyth meets the Traveler and calls them the Savior; Iansan finds it troubling that she seems to regard the Abyss Order's leader, the Traveler's sibling, as a Savior too. Dainsleif is startled that anyone still believes the myth after the Cataclysm and explains the title's origin. Haden says everyone prayed for the Savior when the Cataclysm first struck, but the heir was nowhere to be found.

In a time-crossing scene Direidyth, still in her own time near the Cataclysm, asks the Traveler for a memento to prove they are searching for their twin. The sibling later says Direidyth did bring them news of the Traveler and a sight of the Hibernation Chamber key, which is why they left Khaenri'ah; they suspect Istaroth, Ruler of Time, had a hand in the meeting.

Accounts: - Irmin and the court: the heir is a Savior who will bring prosperity (as presented at the ceremony).
- Dainsleif (5.7): "Savior" was a celebratory title given by believers in the court's rhetoric.
- Haden (Abyss Order, 5.7): the Savior was prayed for and absent when the Cataclysm began.
- Direidyth (5.7): a village sage told of a Savior appearing near doomsday; she believes the Traveler could be that Savior.

- The heir (5.7): they were preparing to fight the Cataclysm when they received news of the Traveler and chose to go to them; they cite this as the reason they have devoted themselves to restoring the nation.

Open questions: - Whether the Savior idea predates the heir's arrival or was framed to fit it is not stated.
- How or why the Universitas Magistrorum is said to have predicted the twins' arrival is unresolved.
- Why Direidyth's village kept the Savior story is not explained.

Connections: Fall of Khaenri'ah and the Five Sinners; the Traveler's origin and the sibling's goals; Dainsleif; the Abyss Order; the Natlan chapter "A Space and Time for You".

243.content:
Khaenri'ah's "Savior" is the celebratory title given to the Traveler's twin, the crown Prince/Princess of Khaenri'ah, by those who believed the court's rhetoric that the heir would bring prosperity and rescue the kingdom. It failed: Irmin used the heir as a vessel for Abyssal power, and the Cataclysm followed. Khaenri'ahn descendants such as Direidyth still look for a golden-haired Savior.

Dainsleif and the Abyss Order's Haden both discuss the title in the Natlan chapter.

244.content: Direidyth is a young Khaenri'ahn woman, a quest-exclusive NPC in the Natlan chapter, who sets out from her village to find the Savior her grandmother and a sage described. She calls the Traveler the Savior. In a time-crossing scene she asks for a memento to show the Traveler's twin that the Traveler is searching for them; the sibling says her news pushed them to leave Khaenri'ah when it needed them.

245.content:
Tatarigami (also: Tatarigami curse, Curse God, Orobashi's curse, the curse of Yashiori Island): The Tatarigami ("curse god") is the curse left behind by the serpent god Orobashi, slain by Ei on Yashiori Island near the end of the Archon War. Suppressed for ages by wards called Narukami Pillars, it broke loose shortly before the Traveler's arrival, when the wards on the island were destroyed. It brings perpetual thunderstorms, withered crops, and untreatable sickness and madness. The Traveler helps repair the wards in Orobashi's Legacy.

It is the reason Yashiori Island is in chaos in Chapter II and a stalemate between the Shogun's Army and the Watatsumi Army. It also shows up in the Mikage Furnace at Tatarasuna and in the sword Kagotsurube Isshin.

Established: - The Tatarigami formed from Orobashi's will and power after its divine body was shattered. The item text for the Golden Branch of a Distant Sea says the god's ichor turned into plasma and its will became a curse that could never be extinguished.
- When the wards suppressing it are disrupted, it causes sickness and calamity around the island.
- It appears as a black aura on some enemies and as a persistent storm over Yashiori Island.

- Affected areas have unending thunderstorms, and crops grown in tainted soil wither.
- In people it causes illness that cannot be treated: bleeding, fevers, migraines, rashes, dizziness and weakness. Mental effects include voices and madness; many afflicted talk about a terrifying god called 'Him'. Washizu, Higi Village's chief, describes it as having eighteen pairs of red eyes. Vision bearers and others sensitive to elements are less affected.
- After Orobashi's death, the Raiden Shogun placed wards, the Narukami Pillars, to subdue it. The Yashiori Guardians, led by Kitain Bunsou and the Kitain Clan, took up the work of suppressing it.
- Before the Traveler's arrival the wards were destroyed, the Tatarigami returned, and the conflict between the Shogun's Army and the Watatsumi Army stalled. Higi Village was almost abandoned: only Yasumoto and Chouji remained unharmed, and the chief had gone mad.

- The Kitain bloodline had died out by then (per Orobashi's Legacy Part V), and Kujou Takayuki ignored Kujou Masahito's reports about how bad the situation was. A Kujou expedition sent to investigate was lost, its Lost Texts at Fort Fujitou, Musoujin Gorge, Serpent's Head, Higi Village and Fort Mumei describing its members slowly succumbing.
- In Orobashi's Legacy, Kaji, a resident, and the Traveler repair the Narukami Pillars at Fort Fujitou, Serpent's Head, Jakotsu Mine and Fort Mumei. Each repair clears the Tatarigami in its region; the last, at Fort Mumei, ends the island's constant storm.
- In recent years the Tenryou Commission had the Mikage Furnace built at Tatarasuna using Fontaine technology that harnesses Tatarigami energy to smelt Jade Steel. The Grand Narukami Shrine's priestesses objected that the Tatarigami is too dangerous. In Tatara Tales, the Traveler helps Xavier repair the furnace's damaged core and fend off Fatui who want to use it.

- Objects can carry it. Akame Kanenaga used the Tatarigami to put his consciousness into Kagotsurube Isshin, a blade he made in exile in Snezhnaya, wishing to prove the Isshin Art still deserved the Shogun's trust. The blade's hatred twisted that wish into rivalling the gods and it possessed many people on its way back to Inazuma (Ere the End, a Glance Back).
- Chouji's mother stayed clear-minded despite falling ill; Yasumoto believed the Tatarigami's energy flowed freely within her instead of corrupting her.
- Real-world note (wiki trivia): in Shinto, tatarigami are gods or spirits that bring calamity unless appeased. This is an etymology, not an in-universe fact.

Accounts: - **Orobashi's end.** According to the Orobashi sources, it invaded Yashiori Island out of the desperation of its starving followers and was slain by Ei with the Musou no Hitotachi; the blow opened Musoujin Gorge. The curse followed from its death.
- **How the wards fell.** A note found on the island shows a radical group within the Watatsumi Army, without Kokomi's knowledge, disguised as Shogunate troops and broke the wards, hoping to restore Orobashi's dignity. They instead set loose the Tatarigami.

- **Fatui involvement.** The wiki states that a Fatui mole named Nathan, acting on the First Lord Harbinger's orders to prolong the war, pushed the Orobashi fanatics. This rests on a few quest texts; see `uncertainties`.
- **The Narukami Shrine's view.** Its priestesses hold the Tatarigami to be too dangerous to use; the Tenryou Commission treated it as an energy source.
- **Akame's view.** An item text for the blade quotes a view that the Tatarigami is pure malice against mortal desire.

Open questions: Canon does not explain what the Tatarigami is beyond Orobashi's lingering will and power, who 'Him' is, or why some people resist it. It does not link the curse to any other phenomenon. See `uncertainties`. No sources read show the Tatarigami returning in 6.x or 7.0-7.1.

Connections: - **Orobashi**: the god whose remains and will it is.
- **Yashiori Island**: where its effects are felt, including Higi Village and Fort Mumei.
- **Sakoku Decree and Vision Hunt Decree**: the tension from the decrees fed the war that led to the wards being broken.
- **Narukami Pillars**: the wards that hold it back.

- **Mikage Furnace and Tatarasuna**: the site where its energy was put to industrial use.
- **Kagotsurube Isshin and Akame Kanenaga**: the cursed blade.

Timeline: - Near the end of the Archon War: Orobashi is slain on Yashiori Island; the Tatarigami arises. Ei places the Narukami Pillars; the Kitain Clan guard the island.
- Later: the Mikage Furnace is built at Tatarasuna using Fontaine technology.
- Shortly before 2.0: the wards are broken, the Tatarigami returns, and Higi Village is abandoned.
- 2.0: Orobashi's Legacy (wards repaired) and Tatara Tales (furnace saved).
- 2.8: the sword Kagotsurube Isshin is released with its Tatarigami-tainted backstory.

246.content: Stone lantern wards on Yashiori Island created to suppress the Tatarigami. They crackle with black and purple energy when broken. Parts I to V of Orobashi's Legacy repair the pillars at Fort Fujitou, Serpent's Head, Jakotsu Mine and Fort Mumei.

247.content: The village on Yashiori Island devastated by the Tatarigami. Most inhabitants fled to neighbouring islands or died of illness or madness; Yasumoto and Chouji remain, and the chief Washizu has lost his mind.

248.content: Built at Tatarasuna by the Tenryou Commission with Fontaine technology that uses Tatarigami energy to smelt Jade Steel. Its core was close to meltdown before the Traveler helped repair it in Tatara Tales; the Grand Narukami Shrine opposed its use.

249.content: A blade forged in Snezhnaya by the exiled swordsmith Akame Kanenaga, who failed to become head blacksmith. His wish was imbued into the sword by the Tatarigami, which twisted it into a hatred that possessed people on its journey back to Inazuma.

250.content:
Teyvat Chapter Storyline Preview: Travail (also: Travail, Teyvat Chapter Storyline Preview, Storyline Preview Travail, Archon Quest preview trailer, Footprints trailer): Travail is an official preview video for the Archon Quest, released on 27 September 2020 and narrated by Dainsleif. He gives each nation one or two ominous lines, shows one character per nation, and ends by speaking to the Traveler in a field of flowers. Its opening claim is that the war "has already begun" as "a continuation of past battles" (which the wiki links to the Cataclysm).

Each nation from Mondstadt to Snezhnaya appears as an "Act" with a Latin motto (labelled by the wiki as Ancient Teyvat Script) and a title that became the matching Archon Quest chapter title; a final unnumbered act ("ACT.??") covers Khaenri'ah without a motto. It laid out the planned run of the story from Mondstadt to Snezhnaya, with Khaenri'ah last. Some of its lines only became understandable years later.

The video is best treated as in-world-flavoured foreshadowing delivered by Dainsleif, not as a neutral summary. It shows what he wants the Traveler to consider, not the full truth of any nation's story.

Established: - Dainsleif narrates. The Traveler (Aether and Lumine, both shown) and a field of Inteyvat flowers frame the video.
- Opening: the war has already begun, a continuation of past battles. The gods tempt mortals with seven "treasures" and "the doorway to divinity", while burnt remains lie buried deep in the world as a warning to trespassers. "That throne in the sky is not reserved for you."
- Each act pairs a nation with one featured character and a short line about its god.

Act by act, as the video gives them:

- **Prologue, Mondstadt** (Diluc; "The Outlander Who Caught the Wind"; motto: my freedom is my song). The dragon who defended Mondstadt for a millennium finally faces his perturbation. What does freedom mean when a god demands it?
- **Chapter I, Liyue** (Ningguang; "Farewell, Archaic Lord"; motto: let the contract be made, though the heavens fall). The God of Contracts is slaughtered as his people watch in horror, and in the end signs "the contract to end all contracts".
- **Chapter II, Inazuma** (Kamisato Ayaka; "Omnipresence Over Mortals"; motto: perpetual, perennial, impervious). The immortal Shogun's Bakufu rules eternal. What do mortals see of the eternity their god pursues?
- **Chapter III, Sumeru** (Cyno; "Truth Amongst the Pages of Purana"; motto: light of wisdom under the flowers). The God of Wisdom's enemy is wisdom itself. In the city of scholars there is a push for folly, and the god makes no argument against it.
- **Chapter IV, Fontaine** (Lyney and Lynette; "Masquerade of the Guilty"; motto: justice conquers all). The God of Justice lives for the spectacle of the courtroom and seeks to judge other gods, yet knows not to make an enemy of the divine.
- **Chapter V, Natlan** (Iansan; "Incandescent Ode of Resurrection"; motto: rise, O strong man, and go to your destined victory). The rules of war are woven in the womb: victors burn bright, losers turn to ash. When the God of War shares this secret with the Traveler, she has her reasons.
- **Snezhnaya** (Pulcinella and followers; "Everwinter Without Mercy"; motto: I, nigh unmatched Queen by my glory, shall be guide). A god with no love left for her people, nor they for her. Her followers hope only to be on her side when she rebels against the divine.
- **Khaenri'ah** ("The Dream Yet to Be Dreamed"; Dainsleif is shown). Most people in a sheltered eternity are content to live and not to dream, but in places the gods do not watch there are those who dream of dreaming. Dainsleif says humans have their humanity and will defy the world with a power from beyond.

The ending is addressed to the Traveler as the one "who has set foot in this world". A figure stands in silhouette in the Sea of Flowers at the End. Dainsleif says the journey has reached its end but one doorway remains, and invites the Traveler to step forward if they have understood the meaning of the journey. He asks to be defeated, or commanded to step aside, as proof that the Traveler is worthier than he to rescue "her", and then says the threads of all fate will be theirs to re-weave. His last line says his memory has all but faded but he will always remember how much she, too, loved these flowers.

The video opens with Aether saying there was no time to say goodbye, so let's not call it that, while two shooting stars cross the sky.

Details worth keeping straight:
- The wiki notes that Diluc, Ningguang and Kamisato Ayaka each have a residence that can be entered in game (the Dawn Winery, the Jade Chamber and the Yashiro Commission headquarters), while Lyney and Lynette's home (the Hotel Bouffes d'ete, visible in the open world) cannot be entered and Iansan's residence is not in the open world. This is a wiki observation about game design, not story canon.
- The video introduced a musical motif for each nation that the game reused later, according to the wiki.
- The line about the "throne in the sky" plays on the Chinese use of the word for "throne" in constellation names; the English cannot carry the pun.
- The Sumeru act title is a Purana-style title in Chinese (about the "Akasha Calamity Ash"), and the "folly" line puns on the Fatui's Chinese name. Both wordplays were lost in the early English version.

Accounts: Dainsleif is the only voice. He speaks as someone who disapproves of the gods' order and, in the Khaenri'ah act, counts himself among the "we" who will defy the world. He frames the gods as offering rewards while keeping mortals from the divine throne, and humans as people who should defy that. The video shows no counter-view, and later canon complicates several of his claims, so he should not be treated as an objective narrator.

The Chinese original is more literal than the English release. Examples from the wiki's unofficial translation: the gods "encase the outlines of desire in seven types of brilliant light" to show their authority can be exceeded; the Mondstadt dragon is a giant who guarded the city of freedom for thousands of years rather than "a millennium"; and the Heavenly Principles are the one thing the Fontaine god cannot make her enemy. The Natlan and Snezhnaya acts are phrased differently in Chinese ("rules of war carved into the bodies of all living things"; "a god whom no one will love ever again").

The Snezhnaya act says her followers follow because they believe she will one day raise a flag of rebellion against the Heavenly Principles. This is how Dainsleif describes it, not necessarily how the Fatui would describe it.

Connections: - The acts line up with the Archon Quest chapters named in the video.
- The Fontaine act's courtroom drama and judging of gods fits Fontaine's central story, covered in the Prophecy of Fontaine entry.
- The opening ("past battles", which the wiki links to the Cataclysm) and the Khaenri'ah act tie the nation acts to the Khaenri'ah thread, and the ending's challenge to "rescue her" points toward the Traveler's journey's end; who "her" is stays unstated (see open questions).

Reading the lines against later content is possible but should be labelled as a reading. The "senselessly slaughtered" line fits the Liyue chapter's staging of the God of Contracts' death; what the "contract to end all contracts" refers to is left to interpretation. The Natlan line fits Mavuika sharing an Ancient Name with the Traveler, as the wiki links it. The Snezhnaya line fits the Fatui's focus on the Tsaritsa's rebellion. None of these matches is spelled out by the video, and how they play out belongs to the quest entries.

Open questions: - Which lines were meant literally and which as poetry cannot be told from the video itself.
- Who "her" is in the closing lines is not stated in the video. This archive does not pick a reading.
- Whether Dainsleif's challenge ("defeat me ... to rescue her") promises a literal later fight is not established by the video. His full role belongs in his own entry.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay guidance (this project's recommendation, not canon text). The video was an out-of-game release, so characters would not know it as a document. It is a good flavour source for how Dainsleif speaks (formal, aphoristic, pointedly addressed to the Traveler). Do not give characters knowledge of later chapters merely because the video hints at them.

In scenes with Dainsleif, the tone of the closing address (challenging, weary and elegiac) is canon-consistent. Avoid having him spell out the meaning of the acts, since the video deliberately leaves them veiled.

251.comment: Teyvat Chapter Storyline Preview: Travail: Travail video
251.content:
Travail is an official preview video, released 27 September 2020 and narrated by Dainsleif. It runs through the Archon Quest nations one act at a time, each with a Latin motto, one featured character and a short ominous line about the nation's god. It opens with the statement that the war has begun again and that the divine throne is not for mortals, and closes with Dainsleif's challenge to the Traveler in the Sea of Flowers at the End.

Featured characters: Diluc (Mondstadt), Ningguang (Liyue), Kamisato Ayaka (Inazuma), Cyno (Sumeru), Lyney and Lynette (Fontaine), Iansan (Natlan), Pulcinella and Fatui followers (Snezhnaya), and Dainsleif (Khaenri'ah).

Ducam Regina Mea Gloria Haud Pluribus Impar
252.comment: Teyvat Chapter Storyline Preview: Travail: Act mottos
252.content: Each numbered act in Travail (Prologue to VI) carries a Latin motto, labelled by the wiki as Ancient Teyvat Script. The Khaenri'ah act has none. Wiki translations: Mondstadt, my freedom is my song; Liyue, let the contract be made though the heavens fall; Inazuma, perpetual, perennial, impervious; Sumeru, light of wisdom under the flowers; Fontaine, justice conquers all; Natlan, rise, O strong man, and go to your destined victory; Snezhnaya, I, nigh unmatched Queen by my glory, shall be guide.

253.content:
The Withering (also: Withering Zone, Withering Zones, Tumor of the Withering, Marana, Black Tide): The Withering is a blight in Sumeru that kills living land and sickens people. It shows up as dark, hostile Withering Zones: patches of dead ground where monsters gather and a "tumor" sits at the centre. Its human form is the illness Eleazar. It is tied to forbidden knowledge and, after the 3.2 Archon Quest, stopped spreading, but zones that already existed remain a danger.

Sumeru's people have met it at two moments: in the ancient desert kingdom of King Deshret, and again during the Cataclysm 500 years ago, when the pollution of Irminsul made new zones appear faster than the Forest Rangers could clear them.

Established: - It is a climate-like blight of Sumeru, named the Withering in game. Aranara call it Marana and say it can turn forest (Vana) into desert (Valuka); an old book calls it the Black Tide.
- Zones are harmful to everything living; humans without a Vision can barely endure them.
- Eleazar is the Withering's manifestation in human bodies.

- A Withering Zone is centred on a Tumor of the Withering, ringed by Withering Branches and sometimes Fetid Boughs (budding, flower-like growths that spit at intruders). Dendro power destroys the branches; the tumor then calls up a stronger "Disciple of Decay"; once that is beaten the tumor can be destroyed and the zone ends for good. Creatures such as Tri-Lakshana animals sit scorched and unresponsive inside until it is cleared.
- Zones start as small nascent zones that draw a few monsters; if left, they grow, gain branches and boughs, and begin to affect people. Typical inhabitants are Fungi, Ruin Machines and Riftwolves; no ordinary wildlife or harvestable plants survive within.
- Rana, who did not yet hold a Vision, spent only a few minutes in a zone and left sick and exhausted, then fell into a coma; Arana bubbled her to keep her safe (as told on the wiki page).

- The book The Folio of Foliage (pre-3.2 text) treats the Black Tide as a flood of decay that swallowed fields, villages and cities, whose root lay underground.
- Forest Rangers carrying Visions were the main force against zones, but after the Cataclysm new ones appeared faster than they could be cleared.
- Gameplay note (not in-world fact): the game models exposure as a Decay gauge that lowers resistances and Max HP and kills the party if it stays full; Candles of Life, Flames of Life and some waypoints relieve it.

Accounts: - Wiki Lore summary: King Deshret introduced forbidden knowledge to his people; the land weakened and the blight afflicted those who wandered in. Greater Lord Rukkhadevata checked it, but the effort cost her much of her power and left her child-sized.
- Homecoming (3.6): Apep says she was polluted by forbidden knowledge; elemental lifeforms born from her fled her body, and the wiki reads the Withering as their "death", with the lifeforms turning into Tumors. After a zone is cleared, any life essence left in the tumor can be reclaimed by a living elemental lifeform.
- Aranara folklore (Arakarman): Marana is an old enemy of the hero Aramuhukunda, alongside giant iron machines.

History: It first appeared in King Deshret's desert kingdom, was halted by Rukkhadevata at great cost, and returned with the Cataclysm 500 years ago.

Rukkhadevata sacrificed herself to stop it spreading across Sumeru. Cases fell, but her taint in Irminsul kept feeding it, so it still spread. After Nahida removed Rukkhadevata from Irminsul (3.2), the Withering stopped expanding and Eleazar disappeared, though existing zones stayed.

Homecoming (3.6) then gave a second angle: the blight as the death of the elemental lifeforms that escaped Apep, which Nahida resolved by healing Apep and keeping Rukkhadevata's promise to those lifeforms. Alhaitham had already noticed in Through the Predawn Night (3.2) that the Withering, Eleazar and the sandstorms resembled the ancient desert pollution.

Status as of 7.1: As of 7.1 the Withering no longer spreads, but old Withering Zones can still be met in Sumeru. Forbidden knowledge is considered erased from Teyvat.

No canon after 3.6 revisits the Withering directly in the sources checked. Do not place new zones in a post-3.2 scene as spreading naturally; a lingering zone is fine.

Connections: Closely linked to forbidden knowledge (cause), Eleazar (human form), Rukkhadevata and Irminsul (why it spread), and Apep (Homecoming).

How {{char}} behaves: For scenes: describe zones as silent, airless patches of dead growth with a faint sour taint, watched by monsters; do not make them spread beyond what canon states. Characters like Tighnari or the Forest Rangers speak of them as a known hazard; most Sumeru residents rarely enter.

254.content: A Withering Zone is a patch of corrupted ground in Sumeru with a Tumor of the Withering at its centre. Dendro power breaks its Withering Branches, the tumor summons a Disciple of Decay, and destroying the tumor ends the zone. Inside, exposure sickens and can kill; Visions let humans resist. Wildlife and plants do not survive within.

255.content: Aranara call the Withering Marana, saying it can turn forest into desert. The Folio of Foliage calls it the Black Tide, a dark flood of decay from the Cataclysm era.

key: seal left behind by the Third Descender
256.content:
Third Descender's Seal (also: Seal of the Third Descender, seal left behind by the Third Descender, Saarelainen's seal): The Third Descender's Seal is a sealed secret kept in a hidden basement of Zapolyarny Palace in Snezhnaya. It is the last thing the Third Descender (Saarelainen) left behind before the Heavenly Principles killed him. Every attempt to open it has failed; only a Gnosis seems to respond to it. What is inside is unknown as of 7.1.

It was first looked after by the Belyi Tsar and is now guarded by the Tsaritsa, Anastasya, who hopes that once the Gnoses (the Third Descender's scattered remains) are gathered, its secret can finally be seen. The Traveler and Paimon were shown it in 7.1 when she granted them access to the palace.

The seal ties together three threads: the Third Descender's bargain with the Heavenly Principles, the Tsaritsa's campaign to collect the Gnoses, and the question of what the Heavenly Principles failed to notice. Canon shows only the room and Anastasya's description, so everything beyond that must be treated as open.

Established: - It lies in a basement room in Zapolyarny Palace, reached through a hidden door that the Tsaritsa had opened for the Traveler as part of the information she was willing to share.
- Anastasya calls it a seal left behind by the Third Descender and says it holds a secret yet to be revealed.
- Its original custodian was her predecessor, the Belyi Tsar, who said it was the last thing the Third Descender left behind before the Heavenly Principles killed him.
- It seems to have gone unnoticed by the Heavenly Principles.
- Every attempt to open it over the centuries has failed. The only thing that seems to respond to it is a Gnosis.

- Anastasya reasons that whatever the Third Descender sought to protect at the very end must be of vital importance. She suggests that only once his remains are no longer scattered across the world might the legacy he sealed away be seen.
- Paimon concludes that Anastasya has two reasons to collect the Gnoses: to amplify her power against the Heavenly Principles, and to break the seal. Anastasya confirms this, and agrees that it will be a while before the answer is known because the Pyro Gnosis is still missing.
- The Gnoses were made from the Third Descender's body, so the seal and the Gnoses are two legacies of the same person.

- By 7.1 the Fatui hold six Gnoses (the Cryo Gnosis plus five collected from other nations); the Pyro Gnosis is the only one whose whereabouts are unknown. The Traveler tells her it was reduced to ashes with the burning of Irminsul and that Mavuika says it returned to the Ley Lines; Anastasya replies that, being formed from the Third Descender's remains, it cannot coexist with the Ley Lines for long and will one day be excised.
- The scene follows her decision to stop investigating the Traveler and give them unrestricted access to the palace. The game's text frames the seal as compensation for their cooperation.
- She is open that she cannot read the secret herself, even though she guards it.

- The Belyi Tsar knew of the Third Descender because he had fled into the Shadow Realm before the Heavenly Principles erased all trace of him from Irminsul, and he later told Anastasya about her forgotten past with him. She did not feel it as her own memory and did not trust the Tsar, so what she knows about the seal comes through that same chain. Canon does not say how much the Tsar knew of its purpose.
- In a corner of the same room Anastasya keeps a transcription prism in which she records each day's memories. Pierro explains that, like a Stellar Linchpin, it contains the power of the Third Descender and is therefore free from the influence of certain laws of Teyvat, calling such objects variables from beyond this world brought by the Third Descender. It is a separate object from the seal.

The third descender: Saarelainen, the Third Descender, came to Teyvat from the sea of stars and was the lover of Anastasya and ancestor of the Khaenri'ahns. In the account Rhinedottir gives Anastasya in Act IV, the Belyi Tsar incited the two to open a gate to the Abyss, and the Heavenly Principles erased Anastasya as punishment. He negotiated with them: his body would become the seven Gnoses, in exchange for her resurrection and a promise never to harm their descendants. As a guarantee he laid a curse that would send the Heavenly Principles to sleep if they broke the promise. Everything about him was erased in return. The seal is the one thing from this story still physically present in Snezhnaya.

Rhinedottir says the Heavenly Principles saw his power, knowledge and last acts as dangerous and tolerated no uncertain variables, which is why the erasure was part of the bargain. Whether the seal was among those last acts is not stated, although Anastasya suggests it holds something he judged vital.

Accounts: - Anastasya (7.1): the seal was entrusted to the Belyi Tsar, who said it was the Third Descender's last act before his death; she does not know how those events unfolded. The Gnosis response and the hope that it may open once the remains are gathered are her own reasoning.
- The Belyi Tsar (as reported by Anastasya and Rhinedottir): he retained his memory of the Third Descender by having fled into the Shadow Realm. Anastasya distrusts him, but Rhinedottir judges his account probably true.
- Rhinedottir (7.1): tells the bargain, the erasure and the curse, and does not mention the seal.
- Hymns of the Far North: a hymn collection of the Frostmoon Scions with a version of the Third Descender's story, including his journey to court Anastasya and the demand by Pakkaisukko (the Belyi Tsar) that he open the "gates of Pohjola". The Heavenly Principles' modification of Irminsul makes parts of it unreliable, and some claims in it are known to be wrong. It does not mention a seal.

- Skirk (4.2, relayed by Neuvillette): tells him that the Gnosis he holds is the remains of the Third Descender and that it would bring misfortune. This is how the player learns that the Gnoses come from a person.

Open questions: - What is in the seal? Canon has not said.
- Will the Gnoses open it, and are all seven required?

- Why would the Third Descender make something that only a Gnosis answers, when the Gnoses were also the means of the Heavenly Principles' system?
- Why did the Heavenly Principles not notice it?

- Is it connected to his curse on the Heavenly Principles or to his bargain? Canon does not say.
- Is it meant for Anastasya, for the Khaenri'ahns, or for no one in particular? No canon answer.
- Has Anastasya already tried the Gnoses she holds? Her wording, that every attempt to open it has failed, does not specify.

A character may offer a theory about the seal but should be shown to be guessing.

Connections: - The Tsaritsa's plan: the seal is one of the two reasons Anastasya gives for collecting the Gnoses.
- The Gnoses and Saarelainen: the seal's only known point of response is the material of the Third Descender's remains.
- The dormancy of the Heavenly Principles: Anastasya infers in 7.1 that his curse is why they sleep.
- The Belyi Tsar: the seal's first custodian.

- Stellar Linchpins: Fatui research ties them to Saarelainen's remains. No canon says the seal is a Stellar Linchpin or related to them.
- Zapolyarny Palace: the seal lies in a hidden basement below the palace where the Tsaritsa rules.

How {{char}} behaves: Archive recommendation, not canon: treat the seal as a guarded matter that Anastasya shares only with those she trusts. It was shown to the Traveler and Paimon in 7.1; do not assume other characters know it exists. Do not invent its contents, an inscription, a voice, a shape or any sign that it is opening. Keep to the canon description of a seal in a hidden basement room.

257.comment: Third Descender's Seal: Third Descender's last legacy
257.content: In a hidden basement of Zapolyarny Palace sits a seal the Third Descender left behind. The Belyi Tsar looked after it first, and Anastasya after him. Nobody has been able to open it, and only a Gnosis appears to react to it. Its contents are unknown as of 7.1.

258.comment: Third Descender's Seal: Remains of the Third Descender
258.content: Skirk revealed in 4.2 that a Gnosis is part of the Third Descender's remains. In 7.1 Anastasya connects the Gnoses with the seal: since only a Gnosis seems to react to it, she hopes that gathering them all will let its secret be seen. This is her reasoning, not a proven fact.

259.content:
Thunderbird Civilization (also: Thunderbird tribe, tribe of Tsurumi Island, ancient tribe of the Thunderbird, Tsurumi Island tribe, Ishine people): The Thunderbird Civilization was the ancient tribe of Tsurumi Island, a fog-bound island off Inazuma. The people worshipped a thunder bird, Kanna Kapatcir, and offered her blood sacrifices. A boy named Ruu, whose song caught her attention, was sacrificed to please her. She saw it as the murder of an innocent and a broken promise, destroyed the tribe, and cursed the island to repeat its last day until she heard his song again. Only the descendant family of Kama survives. In the World Quest series Through the Mists (2.2) the Traveler ended the loop.

The tribe is one of Inazuma's lost peoples and is modelled on Ainu culture; its place names and script follow Ainu words. Its story is told through the Thundering Fury artifact set, the Through the Mists quests and the Seirai Island thread that came before them. The tribe's own people are gone: what players meet on the island are looping illusions and the boy Ruu.

Established: - The tribe lived on Tsurumi Island and worshipped the Thunderbird Kanna Kapatcir, using her feathers to make instruments (Maushiro) that carried sound through the island's fog.
- Ruu, child of the last priest Mata, befriended the bird with his singing, promised to sing again, and was then sacrificed by the tribe.
- Kapatcir destroyed the whole tribe in rage and cursed the island to relive that day.
- The Raiden Shogun later killed Kapatcir on Seirai Island. In The Sun-Wheel and Mt. Kanna, Ruu sang to her remains and the curse ended.

- Religion and society: the tribe held a strict hierarchy with priests and shamans at the top. Shamans offered blood to the Thunderbird for protection and forgiveness, and the people read her unpredictable behaviour as revelation. An amethyst-and-gold hourglass kept by a shaman counted down to her arrival, which was marked by a festival.
- Isolation: people were taught to stay inside the island. Those who left were believed lost in the "sea of darkness" beyond the fog and never returned. The tribe believed the Thunderbird raised the fog to protect them.
- Writing: the tribe used the Ishine Script, handed down through the priestly line, which is why Tsurumi's names sound strange to outsiders.
- Descendants: a family that left before the end survives as the Kama clan; the present Kama (a boatman who carries travellers to Tsurumi) is the only person alive who knows how to make a proper Maushiro.
- The Thundering Fury artifact lore is the main in-game record of the sacrifice. The goblet "Omen of Thunderstorm" is described as the cup that held the offered blood.

- The sacrifice: Ruu offered himself because his friends had begun leaving the island and he hoped it would restore things; Mata also thought the Thunderbird favoured the boy. Ruu died at the Moshiri Ceremonial Site. When Kapatcir came back to meet him, she found his blood in a golden cup on the altar at Mt. Kanna.
- Aftermath: Kapatcir razed the mountain with lightning, killed the tribe and left a curse that would hold until she heard Ruu's song once more. The Survivor of Catastrophe lore adds that Ruu had kept a feather she dropped; Thunderbird's Mercy describes a flower that survived the ash.
- Her end: years later she was hunted down and slain as a monster. The wiki, citing the story teaser Promise of a People's Dream, attributes the killing to the Raiden Shogun (Ei) and call Kapatcir an obstacle to progress; her residue was sealed at Asase Shrine on Seirai Island and took form as the Thunder Manifestation (seen in Seirai Stormchasers).
- The loop: the curse made the island replay the tribe's last ceremony. Illusions of the villagers repeat it without awareness. Ruu alone can see and speak with them and with outsiders, and he has "died" in the ceremony many times.

- Why the Traveler could end it: feathers that fell from the Thunderbird were the original Maushiro, and a feather picked up on Amakumo Peak (the Peculiar Pinion) lets players trigger carvings on the island and see her memories. Her memory fragments show she first heard Ruu's song from her nest through rain and found it unlike any other sound on the island.
- Resolution: Ruu could not leave Tsurumi on his own, so the Traveler used the feather's power to take him to Seirai Island. Because Kapatcir was already dead, the Traveler and Paimon told him she had moved there. Ruu saw the remains of Amakumo Peak, understood the truth, did not blame them for the lie, and sang. A new feather appeared as a sign she had heard him; the curse lifted.
- After the curse: spectral villagers and a "Boatman" appear on the island to take the spirits to a golden land. The Traveler can help them find closure through hidden objectives such as Boatman's Task, and each spirit boards the boat once settled. These are exploration objectives; canon names several villagers (Abe, Ipe, Kina, Kito, Makiri, Una and others) without a full history.

Accounts: Three views of the Thunderbird exist. The tribe saw a protector and oracle who needed blood. The artifact lore of the Thunder Summoner's Crown calls her a monster who cared nothing for human worship. Her own memories, seen through the feather, show a lonely creature who noticed one boy among the many she overlooked. The tribe believed the sacrifice was an offering that served the good of the people; Kapatcir read it as murder.

Ruu's account in the loop is also partial. He knows only the ceremony and believes it must be completed to calm the Thunderbird, and does not remember why it goes wrong. The Thundering Fury lore stresses that he considered his sacrifice an offering, and Mata's role is told by wiki summaries more than direct dialogue. Kama's family tradition, told through Sumida's novel-writing commission, explains the curse mainly through what Kama learned from his ancestors.

Open questions: - Where the tribe came from and exactly when they lived are not stated in canon.
- The link between the tribe, the fog, the fallen "strange objects" and the buried ruins under Tsurumi Island is not explained in dialogue.

- Whether the tribe had its own name for itself, and what the Ishine Script otherwise says, is unknown. The script's only known glossed word is Kama's name, which he says means "a very big rock."
- Why the wiki's civilization page and other pages differ on the date (1,500 versus thousands of years) is unresolved.

Connections: - Kanna Kapatcir (historical.kapatcir): the Thunderbird; killed by Ei and remembered through the Thunder Manifestation.
- Ruu (npc.ruu): the boy at the centre of the tale.
- Tsurumi Island (location.tsurumi-island), Mt. Kanna (location.mt-kanna), Moshiri Ceremonial Site (location.moshiri-ceremonial-site) and Seirai Island (location.seirai-island): where it happened.
- Raiden Shogun (character.raiden-shogun): credited by the wiki with killing the Thunderbird; the date is not given.

- Through the Mists (quest.through-the-mists) and Seirai Stormchasers (quest.seirai-stormchasers): the quests that reveal it.
- Thundering Fury (item.thundering-fury): artifact set whose lore tells the downfall.
- Unified Civilization (lore.unified-civilization): the wiki lists a separate, earlier Tsurumi civilization beneath the island, with murals of Celestia, but its relation to the Thunderbird tribe is not established.

260.content: Ishine Script is the writing system of the Thunderbird Civilization, handed down through the tribe's priestly line. Ruu studied it under Mata. Many of its words are modelled on Ainu, which is why Tsurumi's names (Mata, Kama, Ruu, Kapatcir) sound unlike the rest of Inazuma. Kama says his name means "a very big rock." Rocks with carved Ishine marks are used in puzzles around the island.

261.content: The Maushiro is a traditional wind instrument of the tribe, used to communicate through the island's fog; the original ones were made from the Thunderbird's feathers, and wooden imitations came later. Its name is based on an Ainu word for whistling. The Peculiar Pinion the Traveler finds on Amakumo Peak is one of the original feathers and can activate carvings on the island. Kama inherited the knowledge of making a Maushiro and is the only living person who can.

262.content:
Ruu was the child of the last priest, Mata, and was shy about his singing, often going into the fog to sing alone. His song caught the Thunderbird's notice; he gave her the name Kanna Kapatcir, meaning something like "Great Eagle of the Storm," and promised to sing for her again. When island life worsened and his friends began leaving, he agreed to be a living sacrifice. The Omen of Thunderstorm goblet is said to have held his blood, offered on the altar at Mt. Kanna.

Thundering Fury lore says Ruu believed he gave himself for the good of the tribe and the Thunderbird's blessing. Kapatcir, who returned and saw only a dead child and a broken promise, killed everyone. Details of Mata's own feelings come mostly from the wiki; the artifact text focuses on Ruu and the bird.

263.comment: Thunderbird Civilization: The loop of Tsurumi
263.content:
Kapatcir's curse made the island relive the last ceremony endlessly. Illusions of the villagers go through it unaware; Ruu is the only one who perceives change, including hilichurls and rifthounds that did not exist in his day. Adventurers hired by Sumida to obtain a Maushiro were drawn into the loop, and the item they brought back vanished because it came from the illusion. The Traveler learned the truth from Kama, destroyed the perches that anchor the ceremony, and finally took Ruu to Seirai Island to sing, which lifted the curse.

The ley lines of the island seem to replay Kapatcir's will at the height of each loop; red lightning and a red sky appear in The Sun-Wheel and Mt. Kanna. Places on the island where no lightning falls are where Ruu hides. Canon does not explain the mechanism beyond Kama's remark that the ley lines reproduce the bird's will.

264.content: Kama is a quest-only NPC who ferries travellers to Tsurumi Island for the writer Sumida. He is descended from a villager, also called "Kama" in the loop, who left Tsurumi Island to follow the Thunderbird's light and lived a long, happy life; his only regret was not going back for Ruu. Kama says "Kama" is a clan name and that his ancestor was from the island. After the quests he travels with Sumida in Liyue and Mondstadt.

265.content:
Traveler Acts (Abyss Order / Sibling Thread) (also: Traveler acts, sibling thread, Traveler's Sibling storyline): The "sibling thread" is the run of five Archon Quest acts that follow the Traveler and Dainsleif as they chase the Traveler's lost twin, the leader of the Abyss Order. They are We Will Be Reunited (1.4, Chapter I Act IV), Requiem of the Echoing Depths (2.6, Chapter II Act IV), Caribert (3.5, Chapter III Act VI), Bedtime Story (4.7, Chapter IV Act VI) and A Space and Time for You (5.7, Chapter V Act VI). Each brings the Traveler closer to the sibling (in person, in a vision, or through borrowed or shared memory) and gives a clearer picture of the Order's aim: to bring Khaenri'ah back.

Across the five acts the Order's project grows from a machine-god plot (1.4) to a curse-cleansing device (2.6), to the Loom of Fate (3.5 and 4.7), to a woven "Atlas of the New World" holding the Ley Lines of a new Khaenri'ah (5.7). The sibling first reappears in person in 1.4, speaks with the Traveler as an intangible presence in 4.7 (a conversation the Traveler will not remember), and finally explains their own choices in 5.7. Dainsleif, the immortal former captain of Khaenri'ah's Royal Guard, appears in all five acts and supplies much of the exposition. The acts are quest-level material: the individual quests and the sibling's long-range goals are covered in their own entries.

Established: - The sibling leads the Abyss Order and says they will not leave Teyvat with the Traveler until their war with destiny is over (1.4).
- The Order wants to revive Khaenri'ah, a nation that was without gods and was destroyed five hundred years ago.
- Dainsleif is a pure-blooded Khaenri'ahn, once the Twilight Sword (captain of the Royal Guard), cursed with immortality.
- The Defiled Statue and Field Tiller plot, the Chasm device and the Loom of Fate are successive Order undertakings serving that same aim.

- In 3.5 the Traveler learns that Chlothar Alberich, an ancestor of Kaeya's family, founded the Abyss Order, and that Chlothar once addressed the sibling as "Prince" or "Princess" of Khaenri'ah, telling them that to his people they had been "the Abyss" itself.
- In 4.7 the sibling says they are racing to unlock the Loom of Fate's full potential before the Heavenly Principles awaken, and that they miss the Traveler.
- In 5.7 the sibling says they made the Atlas of the New World, that the attack on Natlan was a feint, and that guilt over leaving Khaenri'ah behind is part of their motive.

- Khaenri'ahns who were considered pure-blooded were given the curse of immortality; the other humans taken in by the nation were given the curse of the wilderness and became hilichurls (Eide/Chlothar's account in 3.5).
- The Five Sinners of Khaenri'ah (Vedrfolnir, Rhinedottir, Surtalogi, Rerir, Hroptatyr) did not defend their nation at the Cataclysm; Dainsleif names Vedrfolnir, "the Visionary", as his older brother (4.7).
- The Order reached Natlan in force in 5.7, attacking all tribes at once and fortifying its base at Ochkanatlan.

Accounts: - **The sibling**: frames their conduct as a war with destiny. They do not call it revenge, and in 5.7 say that the plan has "only ever been about" the two twins.
- **Dainsleif**: treats the Order as an enemy of the surviving Khaenri'ahns, believes the curse cannot be undone and sets out to make Order campaigns as costly as possible.
- **The Traveler**: judges the sibling's actions by their cost to others, as when they argue the sibling has no right to subject hilichurls to near-certain suffering for a tiny chance of redemption (2.6).

- **Chlothar Alberich** (as "Eide", 3.5): believed that the Abyss would give Khaenri'ah control over everything and that the gods' "gift" ruined his nation. He told the sibling that Khaenri'ah had seen them as the Abyss itself and had looked to them to lead it into that future.
- **Caribert** (4.7): says the Loom began as a means of creating and implanting memories and, once fully unlocked, would create Ley Lines instead. He used the first function to make himself a life as a villager.
- **Haden** (5.7): first claims the Order has already revived Khaenri'ah, then admits he was bluffing in order to get hold of Dainsleif's memories.
- **Citlali** (5.7): describes the Lord of the Night's reasoning as curiosity about preserving a whole nation as an "Atlas", and says there was also a further condition she was never told.

- **Halfdan** (2.6) and the Black Serpent Knights are shown still carrying out Dainsleif's old order to protect the people of Khaenri'ah, even after the curse eroded their minds, so the Order and the surviving Khaenri'ahns are not the same group.

Chronology: Release order is also the order in which the Traveler encounters the story: 1.4, 2.6, 3.5, 4.7, 5.7. The events described in the acts are not in that order. In story order the twins' ship reaches Teyvat, the sibling is made heir in Khaenri'ah, the Cataclysm strikes and Asmoday seals the twins (all before the Prologue); the sibling then wakes, travels Sumeru with Dainsleif and meets Chlothar (the Caribert flashback, 3.5); the Order's Dvalin plot, the 1.4 reunion, the Chasm device and the Loom of Fate follow; the 5.7 act ends with the Atlas completed.

Key dated points (in-game versions): 1.0, the Prologue opens with the twins being separated; 1.4, We Will Be Reunited; 2.6, Requiem of the Echoing Depths; 3.5, Caribert; 4.7, Bedtime Story; 5.7, A Space and Time for You. The thread then continues indirectly: in 6.5 Melanta asks why Asmoday abandoned her for the sibling, and in 7.1 Hroptatyr's parable and the Tsaritsa's account of a hooded figure beside Asmoday add to the sibling's background.
Dainsleif mentions in the Caribert act that his previous journey with the sibling happened in Sumeru, and the Traveler's dream of the stars (the twins' habit of pointing out planets they wished to visit) is the act's only look at their shared past. The Traveler states that Teyvat was the first time the twins had been parted.

Open questions: - What is the "true nature of this world" the sibling says they have seen?
- What does the sibling intend once the Atlas has a host location?
- What is the "final answer" the sibling says in 4.7 they are still seeking, and why do they say they do not know how to face even themselves, let alone their twin?

- The sibling concludes in 5.7 that Istaroth must have arranged Direidyth's meeting with them across five hundred years; what Istaroth intended is never stated.
- The sibling hints in 4.7 that finding the Sea of Flowers at the End was no coincidence; it is not explained.

- What, if anything, did the Traveler lose or gain by losing the 4.7 conversation?

Connections: This thread is the Traveler-side view of the Abyss Order's work. Its goals are summarised in the unresolved-mystery entry on the sibling's goals; the Cataclysm, the curse of the Khaenri'ahns, the Savior of Khaenri'ah and Asmoday's defection are separate entries. The acts also seed the Five Sinners (3.5, 4.7), the Heavenly Principles' dormancy (4.7) and the Traveler's place in Natlan's war with the Abyss (5.7).

The thread links to the Prologue, where Asmoday seals the twins, to the Dvalin crisis in Mondstadt that the Order engineered, and, via Pierro's and Hroptatyr's scenes in 7.1, to Celestia.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay guidance (this project's recommendation): the Traveler and Paimon know the acts as lived experience, but only in the order they happened. After 4.7 the Traveler does not remember the sibling's words, though they carry a photo of the twins with Caribert; after 5.7 they have heard the sibling's reasons directly. Most Teyvat residents know nothing about the Order's leader. Dainsleif knows the Khaenri'ah-side background but not everything the sibling plans.

Do not present the sibling as a simple villain or as someone who hates the Traveler. In every encounter they are affectionate and regretful toward their twin while refusing to stop. Keep the Traveler's responses short and plain.

266.comment: Traveler Acts (Abyss Order / Sibling Thread): We Will Be Reunited (1.4)
266.content:
Chapter I Act IV. After travelling briefly with Dainsleif, the Traveler takes an Adventurers' Guild commission in Liyue about Treasure Hoarders raiding Abyss Order ruins. Inside they find a Defiled Statue of Barbatos hanging upside down and are ambushed by an Abyss Herald. Dainsleif explains that Khaenri'ah never had gods of its own, that its Field Tillers (now called Ruin Guards) were mortal weapons, and that the Order means to attach Osial's limbs to the statue and set the eye of the first Field Tiller in its hand to make a mechanised god. The trail leads through Mondstadt (the Favonius Cathedral, Wolvendom, where the Herald is again found corrupting Boreas) to the Field Tiller in Stormterror's Lair, whose eye Dainsleif removes. Back at the ruins the sibling suddenly appears and stops Dainsleif from strangling the Herald.

The sibling reveals that Dainsleif is the Twilight Sword, a Royal Guard of Khaenri'ah who failed to protect it and now suffers immortality. They refuse to leave with the Traveler, saying their war with destiny must end first, and that the Traveler will see the world's truth in their own travels, as they themselves already have. The Herald's portal carries them away and closes before Dainsleif and the Traveler can follow. Paimon urges the Traveler to keep going to Inazuma.

267.comment: Traveler Acts (Abyss Order / Sibling Thread): Requiem of the Echoing Depths (2.6)
267.content:
Chapter II Act IV. The Traveler takes a miner's commission about hilichurl behaviour in the Chasm and meets Dainsleif again, who tells them that "Twilight Sword" was his title five hundred years ago and that the sibling was his travelling companion in search of their fates. Dainsleif realises hilichurls come to the Chasm to die in peace, because its ancient pool weakens the curse. The group meets Black Serpent Knights, once Dainsleif's subordinates, who still obey his order to protect the people of Khaenri'ah.

An Inteyvat flower shows the Traveler a vision of the sibling and an Abyss Herald planning to magnify the pool's power a hundredfold so as to lift the curse from the gathered hilichurls and restore "the homeland". Dainsleif calls it futile, and the Traveler agrees to help stop it. Halfdan, the knight who spared them, sacrifices himself to hold off the activated device; the Traveler defeats an Abyss Lector and breaks its machinery. Halfdan's soul speaks briefly to Dainsleif before passing on. Dainsleif leaves to recover and to look into the Order's Loom of Fate.

268.comment: Traveler Acts (Abyss Order / Sibling Thread): Caribert (3.5)
268.content:
Chapter III Act VI. In Sumeru, Kaeya (who has stowed away to Sumeru before to learn about his roots) meets the Traveler at Djafar Tavern. Dainsleif appears and says that Kaeya's ancestors, the Alberichs, founded the Abyss Order. Dainsleif then takes the Traveler to a farm and hut in Avidya Forest where he remembers walking with the sibling. There the Traveler meets "Eide", a Khaenri'ahn who is nursing a masked hilichurl named Caribert, his illegitimate son by a woman from Mondstadt. A medicine brewed with Sumeru ingredients restores Caribert for a time.

Eide describes the two curses: immortality for the "greater sinners", the wilderness curse for the rest. The Traveler and Eide follow a hilichurl to a hidden sanctuary and meet a being of the Abyss who is not one of the Order; a voice that calls itself a "sinner" speaks, and Eide takes it for a god (it is later identified as Vedrfolnir). When Caribert removes his mask, Abyssal energy overwhelms the Traveler. On coming to and seeing their sibling's face in a broken mirror, the Traveler realises the whole episode has been their sibling's memory from centuries ago: Eide is Chlothar Alberich, who tells the sibling that Khaenri'ah once believed they would bring new strength and hope, and calls them Prince or Princess. The Traveler wakes beside Dainsleif and Paimon, finds remains in the field and is told by Dainsleif that the voice may have seen them; he leaves to confirm who the sinner is.

269.comment: Traveler Acts (Abyss Order / Sibling Thread): Bedtime Story (4.7)
269.content:
Chapter IV Act VI. Katheryne gives the Traveler a commission to find a missing man whom the villagers of Vimara Village remember fondly, but whose name none of them knows. The Traveler suspects he exists only in memory. Dainsleif, also in the village, tells them that the voice they heard was Vedrfolnir, his older brother and one of the Five Sinners, and that the Order's Loom of Fate keeps advancing even without the eye of the first Field Tiller.

Dainsleif suddenly remembers handing the eye to someone; this proves a false memory planted to make him check on its hiding place. He sends the Traveler away knowingly so as to meet the sibling alone. In the village the Traveler finds the missing man is Caribert, who takes them into his consciousness. Caribert explains how the Loom works, admits that he planted the memory and that the Order now has the eye, and fades away in peace. The sibling appears but cannot be touched. They say they are hurrying to unlock the Loom's full potential before the Heavenly Principles awaken (the Principles did not stir even when Focalors' throne was destroyed), admit they are lonely, and warn that the Traveler will forget the talk. Afterwards the Traveler finds a photo of the twins and Caribert in their pocket.

key: A Space and Time for You
A Space and Time Without You
270.comment: Traveler Acts (Abyss Order / Sibling Thread): A Space and Time for You (5.7)
270.content:
Chapter V Act VI. In Natlan the Traveler finds the sibling's key to the ship's Hibernation Chamber lying near a sleeping hilichurl, and the Order attacks every tribe at once. The Traveler tells Mavuika that their sibling leads the Order. They meet Direidyth, a woman looking for the "Savior"; the Traveler can see the monsters chasing her only while holding her hand, and she can see the ones the Traveler sees only while holding theirs. Dainsleif arrives, calls "Savior" a title the sibling bore before the Cataclysm, and with the Traveler storms Ochkanatlan, where the Baptist, Dainsleif's former master Haden, claims the Order has already revived Khaenri'ah.

Haden is revealed to have been bluffing in order to harvest Dainsleif's memories, which the Order needs to restore the nation. The Traveler and Direidyth realise they come from different points in time, and the sibling arrives. They explain that when the Cataclysm began, Direidyth found them with news that the Traveler was searching for them and showed them the key to the Traveler's Hibernation Chamber, which led them to leave Khaenri'ah to find their twin (they conclude Istaroth must have had a hand in this); that the Natlan attack was a feint while they spoke to the Lord of the Night; that the Loom of Fate wove a superimposed New Khaenri'ah and the Atlas of the New World; and that it still needs a suitable host location; to speak with the Heavenly Principles as an equal they will need the might of an entire world behind them. Citlali later says the Lord of the Night was intrigued and set a condition she was not told.

271.comment: Traveler Acts (Abyss Order / Sibling Thread): Dainsleif in the sibling thread
271.content: Dainsleif, an immortal Khaenri'ahn who was captain of the Royal Guard, hunts the Abyss Order in all five acts. He travels with the Traveler yet is secretive, and disappears when he has a lead. Over the thread he reveals that he travelled with the sibling, that Vedrfolnir is his brother, that his old master Haden joined the Order, and that he gave Haden a hundred deaths for it. He is wary of Kaeya, and says he does not know him well.

272.content:
The Twins' Origin (also: Traveler's origin, the twins' homeworld, Aether and Lumine's origin, twins' lost world, the twins' voyage): The Traveler and their twin once ruled a world in the sea of stars. After it was destroyed they crossed the cosmos in a spaceship, asleep for most of the trip, looking for a world with "potential". The ship passed Teyvat once, thousands of years ago, then came back and crash-landed in Nod-Krai. Item text blames a "star-devouring darkness" for their lost world. Almost nothing else about their origin is known as of 7.1.

Everything here is seen through item text, the 6.x Nod-Krai quests and the flight logs on the Frost Moon. The twins themselves do not remember most of it. For the sibling's later choices see the sibling-goals entry.

Established: - The twins were the rulers of a world, which was destroyed. The glider text of Wings of Fate's Course Intertwined says the sibling went "from the ruler of a world to the hope of but a single nation" in Khaenri'ah.
- They travelled between worlds in a spaceship. The Traveler slept aboard until the sibling woke them 500 years ago, during the Cataclysm.
- The Traveler is the fourth known Descender. A Descender is someone from outside Teyvat whose power can affect its fate.

- The Sword of Descension text says humankind once tried to preserve a "doomed world" that was its "last and only home" and drew a sword against "the star-devouring darkness". The Wings of Descension text speaks of watching the birth and death of stars on a long journey.
- The ship was built to carry a "spark of civilization" to a new world. The 6.3 outfit text says it searched for a world with potential for thousands of years, without success. It was run by a navigational intelligence which kept the twins asleep. They were left in stasis pods beside a genetic vault. The ship could remake terrain, air and ecosystems.
- Khaenri'ah's Universitas Magistrorum tracked the ship. The Achievement: Orbits namecard (4.0) quotes its report to the king that the "two stars" had been captured by the world's gravity.
- The ship fell at Starsand Shoal in Nod-Krai and stayed there so long that it was overgrown and seen by several generations. People tried to strip it for parts but could not even dent it.

- In 6.3 (Welkin Moon's Homecoming) the Traveler, guided by Columbina, finds the ship on the Frost Moon and reads its flight logs. The logs show it flew over Teyvat once before, a very long time ago, without landing, then travelled on for what the Traveler thinks was thousands of years. Some data is corrupted. The Traveler had assumed Teyvat was their first stop.
- In 6.0 (The Dark Side of Memory) the Traveler, helped by Lauma and Columbina, sees a vision of the ship's landing in Nod-Krai. The sibling appears outside the ship and tells the Traveler to leave with them, though the ship's door was never opened.
- In 5.7 (The Key That Unlocks Fate) the Traveler finds in a Natlan cave a second key identical to their own key to the ship's Hibernation Chamber. Paimon concludes the sibling must have lost it nearby.

- In 6.7 (Project Moongazer) a sealed data segment in the Moongazers' terminal plays a recorded reply in the twins' voices to a signal they once received. They say they have crossed the universe alone for a long time, that the signal felt like a bonfire in a dark forest, that they will try to find the sender's planet in the future, but that they are dealing with trouble for now. The Traveler is troubled that the new transmission might attract the darkness that dwells among the stars.
- The Traveler remembers the sibling saying that on arriving in Khaenri'ah they could not recall their past. In 6.3 Columbina adds that the sibling rarely came to the surface and, in the early days of the journey, often watched the Traveler from a distance with a guilty look.
- In 7.1 (Etched in Time) Pierro says Hroptatyr summoned someone from Celestia at the moment he summoned Paimon, and Hroptatyr's earlier prophecy spoke of a golden-haired crowned heir answering his call. See the sibling-goals entry for what this means for the sibling.

Accounts: - **Item text (second person):** the Sword of Descension and Wings of Descension descriptions address the Traveler as "you" and say they came by special means, as one who challenged the world. They are not narrated by a character and cannot be traced to a speaker.
- **The outfit text:** written from the ship intelligence's viewpoint. It says the supernova that killed the planet it passed erupted the very year the twins were born, and then insists the two events are unrelated. This does not say what ended the twins' own world.

- **Traveler:** assumes Teyvat was their first stop, then learns from the logs it was not. They suspect the sibling left the ship during the first pass.
- **Columbina:** can sense the Traveler's and sibling's stories as a Trilune goddess. She says she saw little of the sibling's and chooses not to reveal more.
- **Wiki editors:** treat the "star-devouring darkness" as the Abyss. See the Nature of the Abyss entry. They also treat the cloth-giver in Wings of Descension as the ship intelligence.

- **The glider text:** says the Khaenri'ahn heir was "used as a vessel by which unlimited Abyssal power could be absorbed" and became the "key to the world's near-annihilation". It also says they longed for "a single realm" after losing their own world. It is the only source linking the loss of the first world to their later choices.

Open questions: - What was the twins' world, and what destroyed it?
- Why did the ship pass Teyvat once without landing, and why did it return?
- What did the twins know about Teyvat before they arrived?

- When did the sibling leave the ship, and how did they reach Khaenri'ah?
- Who moved the ship to the Frost Moon, and why was it kept?
- Who or what was the voice that gave the twins protective cloth?

- Is the Traveler's lost world connected to the Abyss that now threatens Teyvat, or only similar to it?
- What is the "truth of this world" the sibling says they learned on a previous journey through Teyvat? It is not clear whether it concerns their origin.

Connections: The origin ties into the Descender theme (the Third Descender, Nibelung and the Heavenly Principles), the Abyss's reach across worlds, the Frost Moon and Project Moongazer, and the sibling's story in Khaenri'ah and the Abyss Order. It also bears on the Cataclysm, since Asmoday blocked the twins' attempt to leave.

Irminsul keeps no record of Descenders, which is one reason the Traveler remembers things others forget. Paimon's own origin in Celestia is a separate thread, though Pierro links her summoning to the sibling's in 7.1.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay guidance (this project's recommendation): treat the Traveler's origin as sparsely known. The Traveler remembers little of the voyage and knows only what the ship's logs and item text show. A Traveler written after 6.3 can mention the flight logs and the earlier pass over Teyvat. One written before 6.3 should not. Teyvat natives know only that the Traveler is an outlander.

Who could plausibly know parts of this: Paimon (who has heard about the ship), Columbina (for the Moon and the ship), Lauma and Nod-Krai locals who saw the wreck, Dainsleif, and the sibling. Fatui and the gods know the word Descender. Nobody knows the name of the homeworld.

Do not give the twins a backstory the sources do not support: no named kingdom, family, titles or ages for the homeworld, and no confirmed "Abyss destroyed it". Also do not decide that the sibling is the Traveler's elder or younger; canon does not say.

273.comment: The Twins' Origin: The twins' spaceship
273.content:
The spaceship that carried the twins is a pioneer vessel shaped like a four-pointed star, white with gold lines and a blue cockpit dome. It is made of a material nothing in Teyvat could damage. It is equipped with a genetic vault and a Hibernation Chamber that opens only with two special keys, one belonging to each twin. A navigational intelligence handled the course while the twins slept. After the Cataclysm it was hidden on the Frost Moon, where Columbina took the Traveler to find it in 6.3.

The ship can reshape a planet's terrain, air and living systems so a civilisation can start there. It made protective clothing for the sleepers.
